title: Mock 2
description: Fresh K-maps, shifts, signed byte loads and array summation.

questions.title: Gates and signed ranges
questions.prompt: Select one answer in each part.

parts.label: Which gate outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1?
What is the range of a 6-bit two’s complement integer?

questions.why: NAND is NOT(AND). Six-bit two’s complement has range −2⁵ through 2⁵−1, hence −32 to 31.

questions.title: Unsigned conversions
questions.prompt: Follow the requested widths and prefixes.

parts.label: Convert decimal 219 to exactly 8 binary digits.
Convert binary 101111001 to hexadecimal, without a prefix or leading zeros.

questions.title: Signed encodings

parts.label: Encode decimal −73 as exactly 8 binary digits.
Decode hexadecimal 96 to a signed decimal integer.
Encode decimal −9 as exactly 2 hexadecimal digits, without a prefix.

questions.why: 73=01001001; invert and add 1 to get 10110111. Hex 96 is unsigned 150, so its signed value is 150−256=−106. −9 is 256−9=247=F7.

questions.title: Unsigned fractional conversion
questions.prompt: Convert decimal 9.40625 to unsigned binary. Use no prefix or leading zeros, and exactly 5 digits after the binary point.

questions.title: Encode a value below one
questions.prompt: Encode decimal 0.15625 in IEEE 754 single precision (binary32).

parts.label: Complete representation: 0x plus exactly 8 hex digits

questions.why: 0.15625=.00101₂=1.01₂×2⁻³. The stored exponent is −3+127=124=01111100. The fraction is 01000000000000000000000; combined fields give 3E200000.

questions.title: Recognising Boolean identities
questions.prompt: A prime means NOT, + means OR and juxtaposition means AND. Choose the valid identity in each part.
questions.why: Complementing an OR gives the AND of the complements. AND distributes over OR. Repeating the same Boolean operand in an AND leaves it unchanged.

questions.title: K-map with overlapping groups
questions.prompt:
Find a minimal sum of products. Columns BC use Gray-code order. Use ASCII primes, no spaces or dots, and alphabetical variable order within terms.
Output F
A / BC00011110
00011
10111
questions.why: Columns 11 and 10 across both rows form a group of four with B=1, giving B. Row A=1, columns 01 and 11 form a pair with C=1, giving AC. The groups overlap: F=B+AC.

questions.title: K-map with corner wrapping
questions.prompt:
Find a minimal sum of products. Both axes use Gray-code order. Use ASCII primes, no spaces or dots, and alphabetical variable order within terms.
Output F
AB / CD00011110
001001
010000
110110
101111
questions.why: The four corners form a wrapping group with B=0 and D=0, giving B'D'. Rows 11 and 10, columns 01 and 11 form the group AD. Together F=AD+B'D'.

questions.title: Flags and directives
questions.prompt: Assume ARMv7 A32, 32-bit registers and four-byte words for this section.

parts.label: After cmp r1, r2, which branch tests signed r1 > r2?

questions.why: bgt implements signed greater-than (Z=0 and N=V); bhi is unsigned greater-than. .asciz emits three character bytes plus one zero terminator.

questions.title: Endian memory reconstruction
questions.prompt: The bytes at ascending addresses 0x0040, 0x0041, 0x0042, 0x0043 are respectively 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12. Treat these as one 32-bit word. Drag or select answers. Options may be reused.
questions.why: The lowest-address byte is least significant in little endian: 78 is bits 7–0, 56 bits 15–8, 34 bits 23–16 and 12 bits 31–24. Big endian reads the same ascending bytes as 78563412.

questions.title: Shift and mask trace
questions.prompt:
mov r0, #0xb6
lsl r1, r0, #2
lsr r2, r0, #3
and r3, r1, #0xff
Enter all values as 0x followed by exactly 8 hexadecimal digits.
questions.why: B6=182. Left shift by 2 gives 728=2D8; logical right shift by 3 gives floor(182/8)=22=16 hex. AND with FF retains only the lowest byte D8.

questions.title: Translate one C expression
questions.prompt: Map each C variable to the register of the same name. Write one lowercase ARM instruction per part; use explicit three-operand arithmetic.
questions.why: Use sub for subtraction, eor for bitwise XOR and lsr for an unsigned right shift. An unsigned right shift inserts zeros at the top.

questions.title: Complete a signed comparison
questions.prompt:
Fill the three blanks so the assembly implements the C block. Inputs are signed; no arithmetic overflow occurs. Each option may be used once. 
if (r1 == r2)
    r0 = r1 + 4;
else
    r0 = r2 - 4;
cmp r1, r2
[blank 1]
add r0, r1, #4
[blank 2]
not_equal:
[blank 3]
finish:
questions.why: When the values differ, bne jumps to the else case. On equality, add executes and b finish skips the else case. The else expression subtracts 4 from r2.

questions.title: Countdown with flag updates
questions.prompt:
Execution ends immediately after the loop terminates. Give register values in decimal. 
mov r0, #0
mov r1, #4
loop:
add r0, r0, r1
subs r1, r1, #1
bne loop
questions.why: The loop adds 4+3+2+1=10. subs decrements the counter and sets flags. Its final result is zero, so Z=1 and bne stops. The preceding add has no S suffix.

questions.title: Signed and unsigned byte loads
questions.prompt:
Assume little endian, four-byte words and an aligned data label. Enter 0x plus exactly 8 hex digits. 
.data
.balign 4
data: .word 0x7F80FE01
.text
ldr r0, =data
ldrb r1, [r0, #1]
ldrsb r2, [r0, #2]
ldr r3, [r0]
questions.why: Ascending bytes are 01 FE 80 7F. ldrb at offset 1 zero-extends FE; ldrsb at offset 2 sign-extends 80 (−128), giving FFFFFF80. The full word load preserves 7F80FE01.

questions.title: Match a conditional block
questions.prompt:
Match this assembly to signed C. Assume no arithmetic overflow. Execution ends at done. 
cmp r1, #0
bge nonnegative
rsb r0, r1, #0
b done
nonnegative:
mov r0, r1
done:
For this question, rsb r0, r1, #0 computes r0 = 0 − r1.
questions.why: bge selects the copy for zero and positive values. Negative values are negated by reverse subtraction. This computes absolute value for the assumed non-overflowing inputs; INT_MIN is excluded by that assumption.

questions.title: Complete an array-summing loop
questions.prompt:
The array has exactly four 32-bit words. Complete the missing load so the program sums all four elements. Write one lowercase instruction using the existing index r1 scaled by lsl #2. Execution ends at done. 
.data
.balign 4
values: .word 3, 8, 2, 7
.text
ldr r4, =values
mov r0, #0
mov r1, #0
loop:
[missing instruction]
add r0, r0, r2
add r1, r1, #1
cmp r1, #4
bne loop
done:
questions.why: ldr r2, [r4, r1, lsl #2] loads the word at base+4×index, without changing the base or index. The loop loads indices 0,1,2,3 and sums 3+8+2+7=20. After the fourth increment r1=4, so bne is not taken.
